analysis.one_liner: Strips federal limits on how long truck drivers can be forced to work.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; hours-of-service rules stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop the Department of Transportation from setting any limit on the maximum hours a property-carrying truck driver can work. In exchange, it would let a driver take at least 10 straight hours off when they tell their company they need rest. The practical effect is that trucking companies could schedule near-endless driving, with a driver's rest depending on that driver speaking up. The bill never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: Trucking companies and freight shippers. Without a federal cap on hours, carriers gain flexibility to run drivers longer without hiring more drivers, and shippers get freight moved on tighter schedules. The bill's one worker-facing term — a guaranteed 10-hour break on request — does little to offset the loss of an enforceable limit, since it depends on the driver risking conflict with their employer to use it.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars the Secretary of Transportation from issuing any requirements on maximum hours of service for drivers of property-carrying commercial trucks [S3].

The CRS summary confirms the prohibition and describes the compensating rule: a driver must be allowed at least 10 consecutive hours off duty in a 24-hour period when they tell the carrier they need immediate rest [S2].
Carriers would face no federal ceiling on scheduled driving time, so they could run trucks and drivers longer per day without adding staff or trucks [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Truck drivers and everyone sharing the road with trucks. Drivers lose the enforceable federal cap that limits how long they can be scheduled to work, leaving fatigue up to individual negotiation with an employer that controls their miles and pay. Fatigued long-haul driving is a documented cause of serious crashes, so the safety cost lands on drivers and the public.

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates the Department of Transportation's authority to cap working hours for property-carrying truck drivers, replacing a rule everyone can enforce with a right that exists only if the driver asks for it [S2] [S3].

The 10-hour rest guarantee kicks in only when a driver tells the carrier they need immediate rest; a driver paid by the mile or facing scheduling pressure may not feel free to make that request, which is the standard objection to making safety protections self-enforcing [S3].
Longer allowable shifts mean more fatigued driving on public highways; hours-of-service limits exist specifically to prevent fatigue-related crashes [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain to carriers — cheaper, more flexible scheduling — is real but comes almost entirely out of drivers' working conditions and highway safety. Rest-on-request is a weak substitute for a hard limit, because it puts the burden on the lower-paid, more replaceable party. The bill drew no cosponsors and no committee action, suggesting the trade-off was not persuasive even in a Congress where trucking deregulation had support.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Highways and Transit subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Mast introduced the bill on July 19, 2022, with no cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit [S5].
No further action was recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill expired without a committee or floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Truck drivers and the public came out ahead by default: because the bill never moved, existing federal limits on truck drivers' working hours remained in force. Motor carriers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Truck drivers, who kept existing work-hour limits

for.name: Rep. Brian J. Mast
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar federal limits on truck drivers' maximum hours; it had no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
against.role: Committee of referral (Chaired by Rep. Peter DeFazio)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Highways and Transit subcommittee and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: There is no record of any support or opposition beyond the sponsor; the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have removed the federal ceiling on driver hours, letting carriers run drivers longer shifts instead of hiring more drivers. The cost falls on drivers' rest and on highway safety, which is why the industry interest runs against the public's here.

industries.industry: Freight shippers and retailers relying on trucking
industries.note: Unlimited driver hours means freight moves on tighter schedules at lower cost. The savings come from longer driver shifts rather than productivity, so the benefit is indirect and the safety cost is public.
